# Phase 21: dense turn ingestion for the tier

[Phase 19](PHASE_19.md) built a multi-turn evaluation and found that rung 5 loses most turns after
the first when every token of a user's turn goes through sparse selection. A post hoc follow-up
showed that reading each turn in one dense forward recovers most of them, but the CPU tier could
not do that: it was decode-only. This phase gives the tier that ability and measures it. It
replaces gap table item A5 as planned (a selector that protects recent history), on the evidence
of Phase 19, with the owner's go-ahead. Questions were fixed in `configs/phase21.yaml` before any
run.

## What was built

- **A multi-token forward through the tier attends to the whole layer** (`lazykv/tiered.py`,
  `TieredCache.update`). For each selecting layer, `TieredLayer.dense_kv` brings the sealed blocks
  back from the pinned host store, appends the current block and the new tokens, and hands the
  attention kernel the same keys, in the same order and shape, that a full cache would. Then
  `TieredLayer.extend` writes the new KV into the tier in bulk, sealing lazily exactly as
  token-by-token appends would. Only one layer's KV is on the GPU at a time, and nothing changes on
  the decode path.
- Why not attend only to the selected blocks during a turn? That is what token-by-token feeding
  already does, and Phase 19 measured it losing most turns. Why not a layer-major pass like
  Phase 17's prefill? A turn is short, so the chunk-major forward the model already runs moves every
  sealed block once per layer per turn, which is the same traffic.
- Rung 9 (`ExactTieredCache`) gets this unchanged, since its mirror follows seals. The int8 tier
  (rung 8) refuses it, because its host store is not exact.
- `scripts/10_ingest_cost.py` (question 4), `scripts/analyze_phase21.py`. Tests: through a whole
  synthetic session, the tier with dense turns gives rung 5's answers and ends up holding the full
  cache's KV bit for bit, under both fetch modes and with turns split across forwards; `extend`
  leaves the same state as appending token by token, for splits that do and do not end on a block
  boundary.

## Questions 1 and 2: validity and reproduction

Phase 19's 20 sessions, schedule and quality kernel, with
every user turn fed in one forward (`turn_chunk` 4,096).

- **The tier gives rung 5's answer on 320 of
  320 turns**, at both budgets, with blocks sealed into
  the tier during every turn.
- **The run reproduces Phase 19's post hoc follow-up answer for answer**: rung 5 and the full cache
  match it on 480 of 480 turns.

## Question 3: what the tier gains

| Budget | Questions | Turns | Tier, turns token by token (Phase 19) | Tier, turns dense (this phase) | Better / worse | Sign test p |
| --: | --- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 6.25% | Chat needles | 60 | 25.0% | 95.0% | 42 / 0 | 4.5e-13 |
| 6.25% | Doc, later turns | 60 | 23.3% | 55.0% | 20 / 1 | 2.1e-05 |
| 6.25% | Doc, re-asked | 20 | 25.0% | 60.0% | 7 / 0 | 0.016 |
| 6.25% | Every turn after turn 0 | 140 | 24.3% | 72.9% | 69 / 1 | 1.2e-19 |

- **At 6.25%, the tier now answers 72.9% of the
  turns after turn 0, up from 24.3%**
  (69 turns better,
  1 worse). Chat needles go from
  25.0% to 95.0%.
  Phase 19 ran the token-by-token tier at 6.25% only, so this comparison has no 12.5% row.
- **The document is still where the tier loses.** Every condition, with turns read densely:

| Condition, turns fed densely | Doc, turn 0 | Doc, later turns | Doc, re-asked | Chat needles | Every turn after turn 0 |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| Full cache (rung 1) | 100.0% (20) | 86.7% (60) | 100.0% (20) | 100.0% (60) | 94.3% (140) |
| Quest-style (rung 5) @ 12.5% | 95.0% (20); keeps 95.0% | 76.7% (60); keeps 88.5% | 85.0% (20); keeps 85.0% | 98.3% (60); keeps 98.3% | 87.1% (140); keeps 92.4% |
| Quest-style (rung 5) @ 6.25% | 70.0% (20); keeps 70.0% | 55.0% (60); keeps 63.5% | 60.0% (20); keeps 60.0% | 95.0% (60); keeps 95.0% | 72.9% (140); keeps 77.3% |
| CPU tier (rung 6) @ 12.5% | 95.0% (20); keeps 95.0% | 76.7% (60); keeps 88.5% | 85.0% (20); keeps 85.0% | 98.3% (60); keeps 98.3% | 87.1% (140); keeps 92.4% |
| CPU tier (rung 6) @ 6.25% | 70.0% (20); keeps 70.0% | 55.0% (60); keeps 63.5% | 60.0% (20); keeps 60.0% | 95.0% (60); keeps 95.0% | 72.9% (140); keeps 77.3% |

  Rung 5 and the tier keep the conversation well; the document is what is left of the gap to the full
  cache, at every turn and more so at 6.25% than at 12.5% (at 6.25% even the turn-0 question, which is
  the single-turn test, keeps only 70.0%). That remaining loss is the
  selection's, not the tier's: the tier matches rung 5 on every turn.

## Question 4: cost

Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, the speed kernel, the tier at a 6.25% budget after a layer-major prefill.
Each measurement starts from a [Phase 20](PHASE_20.md) snapshot restore of the same tier, outside the
timed region. Medians of three, with ranges.

| Context | Dense, 256 tokens | Dense, 1,024 tokens | Token by token, 256 tokens | Dense speedup, 256 tokens | Moved host to device per dense forward | Extra peak VRAM, dense 256 / 1,024 |
| --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 32,768 | 0.20 s (0.20–0.85) | 0.44 s (0.43–0.50) | 13.23 s (12.83–14.02) | 65.9× | 0.88 GiB | 133 / 185 MiB |
| 65,536 | 0.39 s (0.39–0.46) | 0.78 s (0.78–0.85) | 13.67 s (13.48–13.94) | 35.4× | 1.75 GiB | 261 / 345 MiB |
| 130,048 | 0.72 s (0.72–0.79) | 1.39 s (1.35–1.44) | 13.59 s (12.73–13.92) | 18.9× | 3.47 GiB | 513 / 660 MiB |

- **Reading a 256-token turn densely is 18.9× to
  65.9× faster than token by token.** Token-by-token
  feeding pays the tier's host-bound decode step for every token, whatever the context; a dense
  forward pays one trip over the layer's whole KV, so its cost grows with context and only slowly with
  turn length. A 1,024-token turn into a 130,048-token
  session took 1.39 s.
- **The cost is transient VRAM**: up to 660 MiB above
  the tier's footprint at the longest context, roughly two copies of one layer's KV (the blocks brought
  back and the concatenated keys and values). It is freed after each layer, so it does not add up over
  layers, but it is a peak the decode-only tier never had.
- For very short turns, token by token can be cheaper: its cost is per token, while a dense forward
  moves the whole layer however short the turn. Where the two cross was not measured.

## What this phase does not show

- One model (1B), one context for quality (32K), one schedule, 20 sessions. The quality gain is
  measured against Phase 19's token-by-token tier, which ran in a different process on the same
  sessions and kernel.
- Dense ingestion does not fix the document loss at small budgets, which belongs to the selection.
- The cost run times one turn into a fresh restore, not a long conversation in which the KV grows
  every turn.
